source.title: Spectral bias and task-model alignment explain generalization in kernel regression and infinitely wide neural networks
source.authors: Abdulkadir Canatar; Blake Bordelon; Cengiz Pehlevan

record.file_problem: Full paper and supplementary information are present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The study derives and evaluates kernel-regression generalization predictions, including experiments on real datasets and finite-width neural networks. These results bear on generalization but do not test a listed version’s specific intervention or measure.
record.gate_note: The paper discusses prior work on random-label memorization and cites other studies; those are not its own results. The paper reports its own kernel-regression experiments on MNIST and CIFAR, noisy-label learning curves, and finite-width neural-network comparisons. Figures supply most quantitative results; only text-described comparisons are recorded.
record.test_reason: The study tests a theory of kernel-regression generalization, but none of V1–V8. Its sample-size double descent does not test V2's width intervention. Supplementary Figure 8b varies neural-network width, but reports convergence toward NTK predictions without establishing decreasing test error beyond the width required for zero training error.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors attribute kernel-regression learning curves to spectral bias, task-model alignment, and noise or unexpressible target components. They attribute non-monotonicity to estimator variance and show mitigation through explicit or effective implicit regularization in their theoretical settings. Applicability to trained neural networks is restricted to the kernel regime.
record.recipe_differences: The study develops a statistical-mechanics theory of kernel regression and evaluates it on real and synthetic data; it does not reproduce the listed interventions or measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset, task-model alignment, label noise, kernel spectrum, ridge regularization, and finite network width affect the reported learning behavior.

fits_no_version.finding: Under the tested two-layer NTK, MNIST 0–1 discrimination error decreases faster than 8–9 discrimination error, alongside greater target power in leading eigenmodes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Task alignment with leading kernel eigenfunctions helps explain sample-efficient kernel learning.

fits_no_version.finding: RBF regression with additive label noise exhibits non-monotonic error as sample size increases; estimator variance causes the peaks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Noise and kernel-task mismatch can produce sample-wise double descent in kernel regression.

fits_no_version.finding: Finite neural networks depart from NTK predictions at large sample sizes. Supplementary Figure 8b reports that increasing width improves correspondence, and Supplementary Figure 9 reports that ensembling reduces discrepancies.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Finite width and initialization variance affect agreement between trained neural networks and infinite-width kernel predictions.

record.problems: Most experimental curves are figure-based; the text gives few numerical values for the plotted errors. The authors state that the theory is limited by the kernel regime and requires computationally costly kernel eigendecomposition; its derivation also uses a Gaussian approximation and replica-symmetric ansatz.
record.rows_left_out: No results cited only from prior studies were included. Other figure-only experiments and analyses in Figs. 3–6 and supplementary figures were left out because they concern synthetic kernel-regression settings or detailed theory rather than the listed claim versions.

untested.parts: Paired natural-label and fixed random-label classification experiments, including training fit and held-out accuracy relative to chance.
Whether widening beyond the width required for zero training error continues lowering test error. Supplementary Figure 8b's improved NTK correspondence does not establish this.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under specified tuning budgets; using Adam alone supplies no comparison.
Batch-size comparisons with fixed epoch budgets and adaptations to the training recipe.
Dropout interventions and their effects on held-out error.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, generalization gaps, and comparisons with norm- or margin-based measures.
Removal of memorized examples versus equally sized random removals followed by retraining.

record.verdict_notes: States are cannot_determine relative to V1–V8 because all rows measure other effects; this does not mean the reported kernel-regression findings are absent. No additional result establishing a listed version was found in the supplied text.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test fitting random labels alongside natural labels, or compare their held-out accuracy.
Does not test whether widening past the zero-training-error threshold lowers test error.
Does not compare convolutional with fully connected networks.
Does not compare adaptive optimizers with SGD on held-out performance.
Does not measure magnitude-aware sharpness or compare it with norm- or margin-based measures.
